Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia) moved for :
Correspondence and papers respecting the extension of the command of Lieutenant-Colonel R. W. Gregory, commanding officer of the 2nd Dragoons, his subsequent resignation, &c.
He said : These papers were asked for by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. It. L. Borden). I have them here and, if the resolution is carried, will be ready to lay them on the table. I would like to say, in

this connection, that, while I have brought all the papers relating to this matter, I hope this will not be considered as establishing a precedent, because some of the papers are of a confidential character, being reports by the commanding officer upon the efficiency, &c., of officers under him. It is not usual to lay such papers upon the table of the House. I think that in this case it is absolutely necessary that it should be done, but I should deprecate the suggestion, if it were made, that this should be done in every case.
Motion agreed to.
ARBITRATION WITH THE GRAND '	TRUNK.
Hon. CHARLES FITZPATRICK (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 152) respecting an arbitration between His Majesty and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. He said : The object of this Bill is to confer upon the arbitrators appointed to inquire into certain troubles that have arisen between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the government certain powers mentioned in the Bill. These troubles arise under the contract respecting the acquisition by the Intercolonial of the old Grand Trunk from Riviere du Loup to Point Levis, or, rather, to a station called Hadlow, and to other difficulties that have arisen out of the operation, under the agreement made in 1898, of the line between Ste. Rosalie Junction and Montreal. These questions have been referred to arbitrators to be determined by them ; but it has been ascertaned that the arbitrators have not, under the deed of submission, the necessary power to examine witnesses under oath or to order the production of papers. In order to have a full and complete inquiry into the matters in dispute, it is necessary to have the powers mentioned in this Bill conferred upon the arbitrators.
It is, to some extent, in regard to freight traffic-division of earnings ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The question of the division of earnings and diversion of traffic arises under the second contract that of 1898. the troubles that have arisen under the first contract, that of 1878, are as to the use of the portion of the line between Point L6vis and Ohaudi&re Curve. 1 may say that that portion .of the line is divided into two parts. Under the agreement, that portion between Point Levis and Hadlow is the property of the Grand Trunk, while that portion between Hadlow and ChaudiSre Curve is the property of the government. It is provided under the agreement that each party has the right to use the line of the other. But difficulty has arisen concerning foreign freight cars carried over these lines. The government claim that the Grand Trunk had no right to charge them for foreign freight oars-cars belonging to other railways- 206i
carried over the Grand Trunk portion. But the Grand Trunk have made a charge of a fairly large amount on each car. The question is whether they had the right to do that, and whether they have the right to do it in the future.
Is it provided that there may be an appeal from the finding of the arbitrators, or will that finding be final '!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot answer that question off hand, but when the Bill is under consideration in committee, I will be able to do so.

I can understand how necessary it is, with reference to the charge of freight cars, that there should be an appeal to the courts, instead of leaving the matter to the final decision of the arbitrators.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The other matter is of even more importance-that arising under the contract of 1898 relating to the diversion of traffic. It was understood that the Grand Trunk was to hand over to the Intercolonial all the traffic intended for the maritime provinces. Instead of that, the traffic has been diverted and sent to other places.
Sent to Portland.

And some of it to Sherbrooke ; I do not know exactly how it has gone.
Mr. MAC-LEAN. Does not all this go to show that the Grand Trunk Corporation is a rather difficult one to deal with, that it is hard to compel them to live up to their obligations ? We seem to be getting into a mass of litigation with this concern, and yet, it has been entrusted with the national transportation proposition. It does not wish to obey the Alien Labour law : it seeks to build up United- States seaports ; in every way a great deal of litigation seems necessary to compel them to carry out their obligations.
All I wanted to know is whether in these Important matters provision will be made for an appeal, if necessary, to the Supreme Court and ultimately to the Privy Council.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) is aware that the usual course is to appeal from the arbitrators to the Exchequer Court, and from the Exchequer Court to the Supreme Court. House in Committee on Bill (No. 5) respecting the Militia of Canada. Sir I red-erick W. Borden.
On section 68,
At or near as possible to, the headquarters of every regimental division, there may be provided a rifle range with suitable butts, targets and other necessary appliances ; and the Governor in Council may stop, at such time as is necessary during the target practice of the Militia, the traffic on any roads, not being mail roads, that cross the line of fire, and may make such other regulations for conducting target practice and registering the results thereof, and for the safety of the public, as are necessary, and may impose penalties for wilful damage to any such butts, targets and appliances ; and all such ranges shall be subject to inspection and approval before being used; and the owners of private property shall be compensated for any damage that accrues to their respective properties from the use of any such rifle range.

I propose an amendment to this clause by striking out all the words after the word ' used ' in the twenty-first line, and inserting the following in lieu thereof :-
His Majesty shall be liable to make compensation for the death of any person, or for any injury to the person caused by a bullet wound arising from the use of any rifle range for target practice, and for any Jnjury to property arising from such use; provided that there shall be no claim to compensation where the death or personal injury was due to negligence on the part of the person killed or injured, or where such person, at the time the death or injury was sustained, was at the rifle range for the purpose of taking part in, or in some official Mr. KEMP.
or other capacity in connection with or as a spectator of the shooting, or in the case of injury to property, where such injury was due to negligence on the part of the owner of the property.
I may recall to the committee a very sad case that occurred some years ago in the county of Jacques Cartier, at the CSte bt. Paul rifle range, I think it was, where a man named Larose was maimed for life. He sought compensation before the Exchequer Court, and I will read an extract of the judgment which shows a defect in the law in that respect. The judgment assimilated his case to a case of damage on government property. and was rendered under that subsection of clause of the Exchequer Court law.
Every claim against the Crown arising out of any death or injury to the person or to property on any public work resulting from the negligence of any officer or servant of the Crown, while acting within the scope of his duties or employment.
Naturally the judge of the Exchequer Court held that the rifle range could not be considered a public work under this definition, and moreover it could not be proved that the man was wounded by a bullet coming from a rifle made by a militiaman, as it might have come from some amateui practising there. As the judge remarked :
Parliament has made provision for compensating persons for damages accruing to their properties from the use of a rifle range ; but not for personal injuries, and it is not for the court to add to or to extend the remedies that parliament has provided.
The case was taken before the Supreme Court and the judgment of Judge Burbidge was upheld. The judgment of the Supreme Court was delivered by Sir Elzear Tasche-reau who, quoting the article of the Exchequer Court law which I have just read, added :
Moreover it is not proved who fired the shot that wounded the suppliant. It may have been fired by one of the amateurs or volunteers not on duty, who were there practising on that day, with the men having what is called in the case, government practice.
Therefore I propose to supplement the present law so that persons suffering damages received from target practice may be compensated. There is no doubt that a person who stands on a rifle range is in a better position to prove from whose rifle the bullet came that injured him : but the peaceful man who may be ploughing his field a mile or two away may be hurt without knowing by whom he is hurt ; so there is no possibility of the latter being able to claim damages if injured. Therefore, while I think it is proper for the government, as I said yesterday, to organize these rifle ranges, at the same time I think parliament should see that persons who may be wounded while on their own property

should not suffer without compensation lining given.

The amendment suggested by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bour-assa) seems to be a very wise one. He has recalled the case of Larose. It is a pity that this amendment cannot be made retroactive so as to give Larose the recourse from which he was debarred under the interpretation of the Exchequer Court judge and of the Supreme Court. As a matter of fact, Larose was maimed for life. He is living to-day, but it is impossible for him to attend to his farm work in any way. I never could understand myself exactly upon what ground the Exchequer Court judgment was rendered. I understood the judge to hold that there was insufficient proof of the bullet having come from the rifle range ; but in law it seems to me that if Larose had established that the bullet came from a man practicing on the rifle range, and I think he did so, I do not understand how he was deprived of compensation. The government, taking into consideration all the circumstances, gave him an indemnity of $1,000, I think after the decision rendered in the' Supreme Court. But it must be evident that that indemnity could not possibly satisfy Larose for the injury which maimed him for life.
Hon. Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia and Defence) Will my hon. friend allow me to interrupt him ? The department offered Larose $1,000 before he took his case into court at all, but he would not accept it. My hon. friend knows that, because he was in the House when that matter was discussed.

The Minister of Militia is right, Larose was offered $1,000. but he was advised by his lawyer, Mr. Charbonueau. I think, now Judge Charbonneau. as well as by others, that he had a recourse, and that $1,000 was entirely insufficient, and therefore he refused the proffered indemnity. I must say that after the case was decided he accepted the offer of $1,000, but that sum scarcely paid all the immediate damage that he suffered from the accident, there was no compensation made him for the life-long injury he sustained. It seems to me that he made sufficient proof to create a presumption that the bullet which hit him came from the rifle range, and that therefore it was incumbent upon the department to establish that upon the day when he was wounded and bullets were raining all around in front of the range, the accident was not attributable to the men practising on the rifle range. At any rate I think the sub-gestion of the amendment of my hon. friend is a good one and that it ought to be adopted.

I would ask the hon. Minister of Justice or the hon. Minister of Militia if there is no remedy now ? I
understand there is a remedy under the present law.
No.
I was asking the legal authority.
Mr. Justice Taschereau is a legal authority.
He is not the legal authority of this House.

I am very happy to be able to agree with my hon. friend from Labelle for the first time, and I seize this opportunity. It is clear there is no remedy against the Crown unless it is expressly conferred by statute and all the court had to do was to ascertain whether the statute covered that particular injury or not. and it held that it did not. My hon. friend from Labelle asks us to frame a clause that will cover that point in case of future accident V I think it is a wise suggestion, I would support it with the greatest pleasure and I think his amendment covers the point entirely.

I think the hon. Minister of Justice should look carefully into the whole question and see that the amendment is framed properly to meet the case, provided there is no remedy at the present time. He should be careful that it goes on general principles. I do not like to commit myself to an amendment such as that which has been suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have no right here to assume that there is a remedy when the Supreme Court has decided there is none.

There surely ought to be a remedy of some sort provided where a proper case is made out. I presume there will be no disagreement in regard to that. But the amendment must be very carefully considered, and not be adopted in such a shape that anybody who happens to get hurt has a ground for asking to be paid. It will have to have reference to the nature of the injury aud it will have to be carefully guarded so that the Crown will not be obliged to prove a negative. The adoption of a statute subjecting the Crown to damages is contrary to the first principle underlying most of our legislation. When we propose in any particular case to go outside of that principle as between the Crown and the subject there should be a special reason for it, because this is a line of legislation that I would not care to take the responsibility of pushing any farther than is necessary to cover a particular case. The law officers of the Crown ought to be responsible for seeing that the amendment is drafted in such shape as *will cover this case, provided the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence is prepared to recommend that some provision should be made.

I think that in so far as government-owned rifle ranges

are concerned, some provision of this kind would be very proper, but the government is assisting rifle clubs all over the country by giving small sums of money to help them to put up targets on ground which they themselves own or control absolutely. It seems to me that it would not be right to make the government responsible for accidents occurring under these circumstances, and if the clause is so guarded as to meet that contingency, I have no objection to it.

I have not read that amendment and it would be impossible to read it carefully at this time. I assume that the amendment will go to the Department of Justice to be recast and put in proper language.
.Mr. FITZPATRICK. The amendment was first drafted by my hon. friend from La-belle (Mr. Bourassa) who then brought it over to the Justice Department, and it was referred to an official of the Justice Department, the Deputy Minister. I had nothing to do with the drafting of the amendment myself, but the amendment in its present form was drafted by the Deputy Minister. The amendment was first prepared by the hon. member for Labelle and submitted to the Deputy Minister and he sent it back in the form in which we now have it, but as to whether or not the amendment ' goes farther than my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence thinks it ought to go, I am not prepared to say.
Now you want the opinion of the Department of Militia and Defence on it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, when drafting a Bill I want to know what the party who has introduced the Bill has in his mind. My functions are limited to giving effect to the intention of the person introducing the Bill.

As I understand the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence he is willing to assume the responsibility of having a proper clause inserted, whether this is such or not, in so far as rifle ranges which are under the supervision and control of the military authorities are concerned, but not in regard to private rifle ranges where individuals will surely he responsible for their negligence.
That is it.

Will the hon. Minister of Justice agree with the proposition that private individuals who have these private rifle ranges are responsible under the general law for anything happening on account of what they have done ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no question about that. The only object of this amendment must be to meet the special exception which exists in regard to government ranges. Private ranges come under the operation of the present law.

I want to have the question made clear by the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence as to what he undef-stands by government ranges ? We know very well that rifle clubs are organized under the militia law, that rifles are supplied to them by the government, that the rifle clubs form part of the militia and that in case of an emergency they are called to the front just the same as other regiments. Therefore, I say that the government is as much responsible for the practice by rifle clubs as they are responsible for practice by militia corps. The hon. minister is perfectly right when he states that rifle ranges established by private individuals are not under government control. I am not prepared to say that this should apply to all rifle ranges, but when I expressed my view to that effect to the legal authorities I supposed'that the legal authorities when they worded this amendment thought that when they spoke of a rifle range it meant a rifle l'ange under the control of the Minister of Militia. We cannot legislate as to rifle ranges belonging to private individuals. We have nothing at all to do with those rifle ranges. I would like a distinction made between rifle ranges that are controlled by private individuals and those that are under government control. If all rifle ranges organized under the authority of the hon. Minister of Militia shall not be subject to this provision what would be the result ? Suppose tihe government, instead of buying a rifle range at Fraserville, for instance, should rent it, and then supply rifles to a rifle club, is the rifle club not organized on just the some footing as the rifle clubs who will engage in rifle practice at the Montreal range or at the Ottawa range which are owned by the government ? In that case this legislation should apply to all these ranges alike. I think I am not stating too much when I say that we cannot apply this amendment to anything except rifle ranges which are under government control because we cannot legislate in regard to other rifle ranges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: It would practically apply to all rifle ranges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All that are provided by the government.

I wish further light on the proviso which reads :
Provided that there shall be no claim to compensation where the death or personal Injury was due to negligence on the part of the person killed or injured.
So far that is right.
Or, where such person at the time of death or injury so sustained was at the rifle range for the purpose of taking part in the practice, &c.
It seems to me that if a person injured at a distance from the rifle range is to be compensated, very much more should a man be compensated who is taking part in that rifle practice, and who is performing his duty as a citizen in qualifying himself for the defence of his country. I do not think we would be opening the doors too wide if we were to include a provision which would enable the government to compensate any man injured while actually in practice, provided it be not due to his own carelessness.

As an illustration, I may mention that in the camp at Levis last week, a man who was employed as a marker for my regiment was injured by a fragment of a bullet flying from a stone and cutting his wrist. In that case the injury was not serious, but had the fragment struck the man's eye he would have been deprived of his sight. In such a case, when a man is injured in the discharge of his duty, he should be sufficiently compensated.
Is not that the risk of war ? If you followed that up you would have to make provision for every accident on the field of battle, and where is it to end ?
You pension those injured on the field of war.
Every military man who is wounded on active service is liable to compensation, and may I ask : Are men engaged on the rifle ranges considered as on active service ?
He is provided for.
I would take it that when a military man is wounded under these circumstances, he would come under the law which provides compensation for those on active service.
Certainly.

I doubt if the term ' active service ' is wide enough to
cover rifle practice on ranges. These injuries may occur out of camp altogther when men are practicing at the ranges. If the minister will assure us that the term ' active service ' is broad enough to cover these cases I am satisfied, but I am not satisfied that a man who is simply about his every day avocation should be compensated by the government, and another man who gives up his time to learn something for the defence of his country should not bo compensated.
I quite agree in that.

I think it is very likely that the Deputy Minister of Justice, in drafting this clause, was endeavouring to make the clause analogous to the general principle of the law, which embodies the doctrine of ' common employment.' The Deputy Minister of Justice, as a sound English lawyer, very likely had that in his mind when he was drafting this clause. But as the doctrine of common employment is a wholly irrational doctrine, and one which ought not be part of the law, we might very -well adopt the suggestion of the boil, member (Mr. A. T. Thompson) and strike out the limitation, which does not seem to be fair or reasonable.

We have rifle ranges which are absolutely owned by the government, ranges which are leased by the government and ranges which are used privately all over the country. The regular corps, the volunteer rifle companies and private individuals practice on these ranges, if these ranges were being used by citizens, unorganized and acting without authority, then if this amendment carried the government would be liable to give them compensation for injury. In my opinion, individuals who practice rifle shooting without being duly under military authority should not be entitled to compensation by the government. It is only in the case of rifle associations and the organized militia, acting under the direction and control of the government, that damages should be allowed.
Men actually enrolled in the militia or rifle clubs.

Yes; and practicing under the rules laid down. The point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. A. T. Thompson) is a sound one, and I certainly think that a marker or a rifleman who is discharging his duty ought to be compensated, provided he has not been negligent.
Mr. GOUR'LEY. Under this Bill no spectator could seek redress ?
He ought npt to ; he has no business to be there.
mitted to go on the rifle ranges, it is very wrong that they should have no redress if they are injured.

If a spectator were injured by a man regularly enrolled I think he should be entitled to compensation, but if a spectator on a rifle range were injured by a person showing off a revolver on the back of the ground, he should have no claim for compensation.

The injury I refer to is by one of the people engaged in practice at the target. In that case, it strikes me that if this Bill is to afford a remedy, it should afford a remedy to the innocent spec-ator. We are invited by the government to go and watch these public exhibitions, and if a remedy is to bo provided for anybody, the innocent spectator who goes on the ground should be protected. Otherwise you are providing a remedy against an almost infinitesimal chance,
Speaking of the Montreal accident, the law requires that certain signals shall be set up, and that is supposed to indemnify the government, for any accident that takes place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Within the area.
I understand that that accident occurred within the line of the fire, not at one side.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that in some unaccountable way the bullet went to the side of the butts.

On the plan laid down by the department, I think it was shown to be within the line of the fire. I will give an instance in my own experience, in our county we were firing, and the bullets glanced off to the lake. A fisherman came into town in the evening and reported that a number of the bullets had passed by his boat. I told him that it was absolutely impossible, because his boat was four miles away from the ranges. He assured me two of the bullets had struck his boat. The firing was done by a novice, who, instead of sighting over the lower bar had sighted over the upper bar. That man would have been justified in receiving some compensation in case of accident. The incident shows that one cannot be too careful in these matters.
Mr. GOURLEY'. If the proposed amendment is to apply to accidents provided for in the previous part of section 68, the word ' any ' should be made ' such ' ; otherwise the clause is ample enough to apply to any rifle range. I think the Minister of Justice will see at once the necessity of that change.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are a few general principles to be borne in mind in connection with this matter. The first is

that generally speaking the Crown is absolutely free from any claim or damages. The principle has been departed from by an amendment to the Exchequer Court Act, which provides, speaking from memory, that the Crown is liable with respect to injuries done on a public work. That section has been differently construed in the courts, with the result that when an injury has occurred to an individual not at the time on a public work, there is no liability. The intention here is to extend the liability of the Crown to injuries suffered by individuals wbo are not on the rifle range, but to whom injury is caused by reason of something done on the range ; and in order to protect the interests of the Crown it is provided that that provision shall not apply to an injury which may happen to a person who is on the range. The case of such a person may or may not be provided for under the Act as we have it now ; but there is no intention to provide for that case.

I would suggest that the provision be limited to a range provided or authorized by the department.
Mr, FITZPATRICK. When an expert draughtsman draws a clause like this, I must admit that I do not like to touch it without consulting him.

As the section reads now, I think it would be much wider than is intended. Suppose a club of private parties provide ranges for themselves and go shooting ; if you do not qualify the clause, you take the responsibility of injuries from them and put it on the Crown. That is a case which I apprehend we do not intend to cover. Suppose men commence shooting on a range before it has been inspected and approved ; the individual who has violated the law would be free, and the government would be made responsible.
Mr. FITZPATRICK! I think that it would be a very great straining to make the government responsible for anything that might happen at these unauthorized ranges. But we might easily avoid any difficulty by making this provision applicable only to the rifle ranges provided for by section 08 and which are under the control of the government.

If a government , range is being used by men who are not regularly enrolled in the militia or members of any rifle association, acting under the statutes of Canada, and an accident happens,
I do not think the government should be responsible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Why not ?

Because these men practicing on that range do not belong to the militia or to any government rifle association.
(5477

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend has in mind strangers coming to a rifle range-
Not foreigners.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be quite right in using that word under certain circumstances.
Outsiders.
That is better.
Do not use that word ' foreigner.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I could point out to my friend in the Patent Act and dozens of Acts passed in this House the application of the word ' foreigner ' to British subjects. In fact, it is the correct grammatical expression to use in certain circumstances. My hon. friend has in view the contingency that men not connected with the militia might use a rifle range and cause an accident, and he says that in such case the government should not be held liable. But a rifle range under the control of the government has to be regulated and controlled in some way, so that every passerby cannot make use of it. If my hon. friend has a piece of property, he does not allow every Tom, Dick and Harry to go in and use it at his sweet will. He controls his own property, and it would be the business of the government to control that rifle range in such a way that no one could use it except under certain regulations. I think there are guardians to these ranges.
But there are other ranges which are not the property of the government, but which are subsidized by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Do these come within the meaning of the section ?
Yes.

Would such a range come within the meaning of a rifle range as described in section 68 ' at or near as possible to the headquarters of every regimental division, there may be provided a rifle range with suitable butts, targets and other necessary appliances.
That covers it exactly. Take the case in my county. The government gave us assistance to establish the butts, but ninety dollars out of every hundred came out of the pockets of the boys.
Is your headquarters near the rifle range ?

Yes. In rear of these ranges there is a line of lire, and that line gets wider the further back it goes. We have to rent land from the farmers and give them notice every time we are using the range. And immediately in rear of the butts, where a wagon road crosses the line of fire, we station a man who signals us whenever
a team approaches. But supposing somebody, who does not know the rules should practice on that range and an accident happen, who would be responsible ? We cannot afford to keep a guardian on that range all the year round.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would be easy to draw an amendment which would make the Act applicable to only one class of range.
But I want it to applv to both classes whenever the range is being used by an official body. In such cases the government should be responsible.

There are lots of rifle clubs which are not headquarter clubs at all. There are four or five in my county that have nothing to do with the militia but are rifle clubs coming under the Militia Act. I have had complaints come to me concerning these clubs under the impression that the Militia Departmnt had control of them. These clubs do the best they can, but as a rule they can only get short ranges, and if the government wish to encourage these clubs, they should put them under some control. But if you were to make the government responsible for anything that might happen at any of these ranges, that might have the result of making those using them more careless.
I can only say I should hope not.
Not unless they are taken over by the department.

Because you can see at once what the result will be. If institutions mentioned by my hon. friend engage in rifle shooting on what may be called private ranges, they take every precaution to prevent injury to others. But if you make the government responsible, there will be much less care exercised ; there will be much greater danger to the people and much greater expense to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I see a way to meet the difficulty-by omitting the beginning of the paragraph and making this apply to rifle ranges of a certain description. as, ' Headquarters ' ranges or other designation to be supplied by the Department of Militia.

The hon. minister however, must not overlook this danger- and this is a matter rather for the Minister of Militia than for the Minister of Justice- if you are going to protect one class of legalized clubs and not others, you will kill the others. As I said in the commencement, this is a matter that requires very careful consideration. If the Minister of Justice is to prepare a proper provision on this subject, he must be seized of the facts ; he must know what sort of clubs are in existence and what sort of clubs the Minister of Militia intends to form. I do not see

liow we are going to make a distinction between one kind and another unless we make it a genera] principle of law. I agree with the hon. member for Labelie (Mr. Bou-rassa) that his amendment is in the right direction, that his proviso must be embodied in the law. But we must not make it too extensive, and we must protect the Crown against the negligence of those for whose conduct it is not properly responsible.

It seems to me that certain words might be inserted which would make the section quite clear ' and ought to make it. satisfactory. For instance, it might read :
His Majesty shall be liable to make compensation upon the death of any person, or for any injury to the person arising from the use of any rifle range for target practice carried on under the regulation of the department of Militia and Defence.
Hear, hear.

By this, it seems to me, the public will be assured that no practice will go on unless it is in accordance with the regulations laid down. In the case of every one of these clubs, there is some one who is responsible for carrying on the practice, and so the public will be protected against injury through the careless carrying on of rifle shooting.

I think the minister has hit the mark. ment's regulations, whether they are built by the people of Canada as a whole or are provided by the contributions of the boys themselves. That question does not at all affect this clause.

Parliament seems to be entirely disregarded in this matter. I am

ready to give large powers to the government for the defence of Canada, provided parliament Is to have a word to say with regard to footing the bill and approving or disapproving of the action of the government.

The only power given to the government is to put the militia on active service. They cannot get any supplies without the action of parliament. That has always been the law, and I do not think it is different in any country in the world. In cases of emergency the militia may have to be called out immediately, but you cannot get parliament together in five minutes. Parliament must be called to vote the supplies, and if the supplies are not voted, what is the use of having a militia ? The power of the government to call out the militia suddenly is one of the greatest advantages to the country. Suppose a tremendous riot or something of that kind occurs, the government can call them all out for active service at once. If the propriety of the government's action is disputed, parliament can deal with it and may refuse to vote the supplies. That has always been the law.

The hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) is not replying to my argument at all. I agree with my hon. friend on that point; but I say there should be a limitation to the arbitrary will of the government to wait for the sanction of parliament. When the hon. member for South Norfolk says that the government would not go on without parliamentary sanction, I reply that that was done five years ago. More than that, it was not even the active militia who were called out ; but a special military corps was organized, and money for the purpose was taken from the treasury of Canada without the consent of parliament. This went on for two months. In all the other British possessions where parliament was not in session, the governments refused to organize contingents without calling parliament. It was only in Canada that it was done. In England, where the sovereign has the right, on the advice of the government, to declare war, they immediately call parliament. They would not dare to spend a pound on armaments without calling parliament. I admit that an emergency might arise when the government should have the power to call out the militia immediately. I do not dispute that ; but suppose an occasion should arise on which Canada would be called upon to organize its militia and send a large portion of it outside of Canada, when in the judgment of a large number of the people and parliament of Canada it would be to the disadvantage of the country to have Mr. BOURASSA.
so large a number of troops sent out, parliament should be the final judge of that question, and the government should call parliament to deal with the matter. It has been done for two months on one occasion, and why might it not be done for six months on another occasion ? A number of gentlemen who did not agree with me on the general principle of the Boer war, agreed with me that it was the duty of the government to summon parliament as early as - possible after an emergency of this kind.

If the hon. gentleman will read the wording of the clause, he will see that the power of the government is very limited. They can only order the militia outside of Canada for the defence of Canada. They volunteered for service and were sent out as imperial troops pnder a special agreement with the imperial government, partly paid by the British and partly by this government, and * the Militia Department organized those vol-1 unteers. They did not come under the Militia Aet at all.

I do not wish to attribute anything to the hon. member for King's other than what he said. Here is what he said :
Whether for the defence of Canada or not, the militia of Canada should not be sent out of Canada without the authority of parliament. There can be no emergency arise under which parliament cannot be called together ; war does ;not spring up in a day or night. If the country were in danger of war, it would be an easy matter to call parliament, and then parliament could decide if it is necessary to send our militia outside of Canada. It
is a different matter altogether about permitting volunteers to serve in any portion of the empire.
That is the distinction which the minister has just made. If, however, there should be an imperial war in which Canadians want to serve, there is nothing to prevent their enlisting into the imperial service.

My hon. friend from King's did not raise that point. He is perfectly in accord with the idea that troops should go outside this country. There is nothing to hinder their going as volunteers outside to fight for the British empire, but if the militia of Canada should be called out by the Canadian government and the imperial authorities should choose to send out a call in this country for volunteers to put down these gentlemen, the allegiance of our militia would be to the British empire rather than to any power in Canada.

There is a distinct change in the Act, whether for good reason or bad. It is not a change of form or words, but a distinct change of public policy in connection with the militia, and therefore we should have the full and particular reasons for such a change. Canada is a part of the British empire, and the militia of this country is a part of the defensive force of the British empire, and ought to be used, in the case of emergency, in India, Australia, or Africa or wherever the necessity may arise.
The defence of Canada might be required to be fought out in Africa, and, to keep the militia in Canada, would be simply a betrayal of the empire ; for the empire might be beaten in Africa, or India, and Canada fall with the empire, without a blow being struck upon the soil of this Dominion. Any limitation of the power to send the militia abroad by a provision that this is to be done only in the case of emergency, weakens our power of defending Canada ; and. at this stage of imperial thought, and development, to have a narrow, and petty doctrine like this, engrafted upon the militia legislation of this Canada, is a reversal of the course of our national progress. When the public man of twenty-five or thirty years ago could engraft on the militia system of this country a broader and more generous policy, it strikes me that we should stand by the position they took, if we cannot improve it. I have under my hand the section of the Act of 1878. Comparing it with the present section, we can see that this is no meaningless change but, that there must have been design in the drafting. It is a

decided change of policy, and one of the most serious character. The section of the old Bill was in these terms :
Her Majesty may call out the militia, or any part thereof, for active seri'ice, either within or without Canada, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of war, invasion or insurrection, or danger of any of them.
So the militia could be called out wherever there was war, invasion or insurrection or danger of any of them-no matter where, the* militia were bound to go. And, surely, that is wise. What is the use of putting the militia under the command of a general officer in time of war, unless he is able to order them to the point of danger, whether inside or outside of Canada. There is, a distinct change in this proposed section, which reads :
77. The Governor in Council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
We do not want the troops sent outside of Canada for the defence of Canada only, but. if necessary, for the defence of the empire, which may, or may not be, directly, the defence of Canada. The defence of India or of South Africa may be, ex necessitate, the defence of Canada. I must draw the attention of our friends opposite, and of hon. gentlemen on this side, to the extraordinary change of policy indicated by these words, incorporating a narrow doctrine that the Canadian militia and troops are to be used only in Canada for the defence of Canada-let the empire go to smash, but keep our troops at home. This is simply closing our eyes to the fact that the empire may be broken, and go to pieces without making necessary any direct defence of Canada, and yet. in that ruin, our interests will be completely sacrificed. We want the old section to stand, as it has stood on the statute-book for thirty years, that the militia are to be used wherever the necessities of the empire demand, whether in Canada or out of it. This is the most vital section in this Act; the rest are merely subsidiary.

Canada either is, or is not a part of the British empire. If the pact between us and the empire is to mean that the Canadian militia is only to be used for the defence of Canada, are we to expect, the army of England will be used to assist in the defence of Canada only to the extent that our forces shall go to their assistance ? That is how the arrangement works out as proposed in this section. Now. that is not an equitable arrangement and it is a decided change in the policy that has been accepted up to this time. undertake to raise a regular army, two or three thousand men, and be prepared to send them abroad for the defence of the empire, I will waive my objection to the militia leaving this country. But, as the member for St. John has pointed out, it is the only militia force we have, and by this section we say we will not lend the only force we have in Canada to the service of the empire. It strikes me that at this time of day, when the empire is so vital to us, when we have infinitely more to expect from the empire than the empire has to expect from us-because to-day, if it were not for the opportunities of foreign trade which the empire offers to Canada, we would b.; desolate indeed-we need especially to foster a good feeling, a feeling of mutual help throughout the empire, and we cannot foster that better than by making our militia force subject to be used in every part of the empire. I urge this upon the minister, because I am persuaded the minister will ruin the militia if he permits this feeling to get abroad that we have changed our policy. I have no doubt that somebody has had a subtle influence in making this change. There has been a deliberate change of policy in changing the language of these two sections, there is no doubt about that. I am too much accustomed to scanning closely this language not to see the distinctions that are made. Consequently, the minister is going to create a strong feeling throughout the country, and I do not wish te - see cur militia made the subject of political feeling. Let us stand by the militia all over the country. But I must say that when that section is read and understood, it will arouse a most uncanny kind of feeling all over Canada. It is not a proper section to be introduced into a Canadian statute, or a statute of any country belonging to the British empire, to say that our poor contribution to the empire shall not be used except within the boundaries of Canada, and rhe empire outside can go to smash. I do not like that; it is a provision that deserves reprobation at the hands of this House of Commons. The old section is a splendid section, and I say let it stand.

I would ask the minister if it is not the case that under the old section of the law as it now stands the militia of Canada could be used for the defence of the empire and sent out of this country for that purpose ? But under the proposed law that is strictly prohibited.
No. I am advised, and was advised at the time of the South African trouble, for instance, that under the law we <;ould not do that.
Could not do what ?

That we could not send the militia to South Africa for service ; under the law' we were not able to do so. The present law has been
REVISED EDITIOIt

changed, as I say, in conformity with that view, and in sympathy with the idea which, as I said, controls the militia of the mother country and the militia of every one of the colonies of the empire, where you will find precisely the same clause.

All I can say is that the advice given to the Minister of Militia does not comport with the law as it stood at that time. The Minister of Militia refers to the old debates that took place when the Militia Act was passed. I am not bound by those debates. At that time men may have had a hard time to get this section passed, and language may have been used, as the Minister of Justice said yesterday, to conceal the thoughts that were in the minds of the people who were carrying this Act through. I say that under this clause the militia could be sent abroad at any time and anywhere that the emergencies of the empire required, and that is as it should be. I can easily understand that the strong and broad men who drew this Act, for it was drawn in the year after confederation, when the fathers of confederation, the big men of Canada, were here-I can easily understand that at that time these men desired to engraft that policy in the Act, and perhaps they were surrounded by little people who were not in sympathy with the measure, and consequently they may have used words to conceal their thoughts, and they were wise enough to know that if they got that section passed the power was vested in the Crown and government of Canada to send the militia anywhere. Not only so, but I say with all deference to the person who advised the Minister of Militia, that it was not legal advice, and if it were, I would have thought that the Minister of Justice would have taken the other horn of the dilemma. At the time of the South African war there was a doubt with reference to the power of this country to send our militia abroad. Let us wipe away that doubt, and let the government have power to send the militia abroad. Let us clear up the doubt on the other side, and make it clear that the militia of this country, upon which we have spent millions of dollars, may be used in the defence of the empire. Now, I ask the minister, if he wants his militia force to stand well with the country, to allow that old section to stand ; then if you have not the power, if the Minister of Justice advises you that you have not the power, no harm will be done. But Ministers of Justice change, as archbishops change, and archbishops very often have different policies in their dioceses, and a Minister of Justice could be given a different advice to that given to the present Minister of Justice.
Might I ask what the provisions of the English Act are with regard to the summoning of parliament when the militia are called out for active service ? Some reference has been made to that.
When they are ' embodied,' that is the official term.
It may be of use for us to have the provision submitted to the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In anticipation of the suggestion coming from the hon. leader of the opposition I may say that during the adjournment, I, myself, in the few moments at my disposal, attempted to find the provision, but since that I have asked one of the officials in my department to look into this matter and get the clause so as to assist us in deciding what action we ought to take.
I think the clause is contained in this book. Just wait a moment.

My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) has called my attention to a provision in the Militia Act, 1S82, of the parliament of Great Britain and Ireland being chapter 49 of the statutes 45-46 Victoria sections 18, 19 :
(1.) In case of imminent national danger or of great emergency it shall be lawful for Her Majesty in Council by proclamation (the occasion being first communicated to parliament, if parliament be then sitting, or declared in Council, and notified by the proclamation, if parliament be not sitting) to order the militia to be embodied.
I suppose that practically corresponds to calling out our entire militia force for active service.
(2.) It shall be lawful for Her Majesty by any such proclamation to order a Secretary of State from time to time to give, and when given to revoke or vary, such directions as may seem necessary or proper for embodying all or any part of the militia.
(3.) Every such 'proclamation and the directions given in pursuance thereof shall be obeyed as if enacted in this Act, and where such directions for the time being direct the embodiment 'of any part of the militia, every officer and man belonging to that part shall attend at the place and time fixed by those directions, and at and after that time shall be deemed to be embodied ; and such officers and men are in this Act referred to as embodied, or as the embodied part or parts of the militia. *
Then section 19 reads as follows :
Whenever Her Majesty orders the militia to be embodied, if parliament be then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall be issued for the meeting of parliament within ten days, and parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation, and shall continue to sit and act in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued for the same day.
PePhaps there are some considerations in connection with the section which we have

been debating that might make it desirable for the government to allow it to stand so as to consider that provision. There seems to be the same rfeason for the provision as there is in Great Britain. Of course we have a separate system from theirs. They have a large standing army ; we have practically no standing army. Speaking offhand and without much consideration of the subject, I would think that while possibly we may not require a provision of that kind in respect to calling out the militia in this country, it would be desirable to have it in respect of calling out the militia for service outside of Canada.
Or for war ?
It could only be called out for service outside of Canada in case of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At the moment when my hon friend the leader of the opposition rose, I received a memorandum which gives me the different statutes under which this summons to parliament is issued.
There may be a later statute than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, that is the consolidation. I find! that formerly the period was 14 days during which parliament had to be summoned and that by the Consolidation Act of 1882 it was reduced to ten days. I think I should have an opportunity to look through the different Acts and see how far it may be necessary to adapt the provisions of the Militia Act of Great Britain to the Militia Act of Canada. We may be required to introduce a new clause. I think there is no reason why this clause should not go through with the understanding that a general clause which may be found proper to meet the difficulty shall be introduced into the Bill before it is finally disposed of.

If this clause is proposed to be pressed at the present time, 1 desire to say I am not quite clear as to what the exact meaning of the proposed amendment is. It reads as follows :
In time of war when the- militia is called out for active service to serve conjointly with His Majesty's regular forces, His Majesty may place in command thereof a senior general officer of his regular 'army who shall be senior in rank to the General Officer Commanding the militia.
There may be some doubt as to what is
meant by the words ' serving conjointly with His Majesty's forces.' Does that phrase mean serving conjointly in Canada or serving conjointly in a general sense in the performance of duties connected with the defence of the empire ?
'Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. It means in Canada.
207i

I would think that possibly even if they were not serving conjointly in the sense in which the hon. Minister of Militia speaks, there might be power given to His Majesty to put an experienced officer in command in time of war.

I think the idea is simply this :	Assuming for the
sake of argument that Canada is assisting the mother country in a war somewhere else, outside of Canada, and not for the protection of Canada, when the Canadian troops would simply be going to assist the imperial anmy and there would be no question about the control of the commanding officer of the imperial army. But, a war might occur, an invasion might be attempted of Canada under which circumstances a large majority of the troops engaged would be Canadian troops. Still, there would be a certain proportion of imperial troops, and in view of the fact that imperial commanding officers have had greater experience it was thought proper t'hat in a war in which Canada would be engaged and in which the imperial army would be assisting, the command should be placed in the hands of an imperial officer. That is the intention.

All I am suggest-, iug is that perhaps the power might be extended so as to apply to a case even where they are not serving conjointly. Suppose that we had in Canada 100 regular troops stationed at Halifax and that the Canadian militia was called out for active service to the extent of 10,000 or 15,000 ; according to the definition of the hon. minister it would be within the scope of this statute to appoint a general officer, but would not exactly the same reason prevail if you did not have any imperial troops in Canada ?
We have another clause under which an imperial officer can be appointed at any time. We are not giving up the authority to appoint a general officer to command.
You did not change that clause ?
No.
I thought you were going to strike that out and substitute a council.
This is one of the results of my attendance at the defence committee when that question was discussed and it was agreed that this special clause would be desirable.
If we have power outside of this clause, what is the object of this amendment 'i

The object is that in the event of the militia serving with imperial troops we shall be under the

obligation to bave an imperial officer commanding. Otherwise it would be open to the Canadian government to appoint an imperial officer, or a Canadian officer as they chose.

If the militia of Canada should be engaged in the defence of this country without the assistance of any imperial troops, it would be quite possible to appoint a general officer of experience to command the militia although no regular troops would he associated with them.
Quite so.

Apart from that there is the power conferred upon His Majesty when regular troops are engaged in this country conjointly with the Canadian militia, to appoint a general officer to command the whole force.
Yes, from the imperial army.
Does not the military council do away with the General Officer Commanding ?
Oh, no. We could not do without the power to appoint a General Officer Commanding ; that still remains in the Bill.

The organ of the new war lord says :
It is a fair prediction that ere the Minister of Militia has completed his list of reforms in that department, the practice of bringing General Officers Commanding from the British 'army to command the Canadian militia will he as dead as>
the family compact.
It is evidently the intention of the military boss of the administration that there should be no imperial officers brought to Canada.

It is quite clear that the old law contemplated that in case of war the militia of Canada should become imperial troops and be under imperial officers. The whole purpose of the old law seems to be to make the militia of Canada serviceable to the empire at any point wherever-their services were required. The minister says that this Bill introduces no change of policy, and if that is so why not retain the old law so that we may be sura of it ?
Would the relationship that now exists between the Cnnaf dian militia and the imperial troops in time of war, be in the slightest altered by the passage of this Act ?
Not in the slightest.
It is held by some good heads that there would be a difference in the relationship existing between the two.
No.
What is the meaning of the words ' for the defence of Canada ? '

Suppose that Canada were invaded it might be the very best means of defence to immediately send an army into foreign territory.
Mr. OSLER, Quite so, but is not the existing law better and more definite ; which says :
Her Majesty may call out the militia, or any part thereof, for active service either within or without Canada, at any time that it appears advisable to do so, by reason of war,
&e.

I think there is no question as to the right of the government to send troops anywhere for the defence of the empire. If Canada wished her troops to take part with the imperial troops anywhere else than in Canada for the immediate defence of the empire, that could be accomplished as was done in England during the South African war, when whole regiments of English militia enrolled only to serve in the British Isles, volunteered for service in South Africa.

Amendment agreed to.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 78-period of service in time of war-

I wish to add the following words :	' provided however that the provisions of this section shall not apply to the Permanent Force.' When we were considering the Bill in committee some time ago, the hon. leader of the opposition called my attention to the fact that, as the Permanent Force is a part of the militia, there would likely be confusion in two or three clauses unless the Permanent Force were expressly referred to. This is one of the clauses.

The minister seems to take for granted that on all occasions on which the militia would require to be called out, they would finish their work in about eighteen months at the outside. It seems to me that the authorities should have a little longer hold on the soldiers.
This is the old law.	,

This is a fair provision, because it must be remembered that these men are volunteers. Under other provisions of the Act, in case men are needed, we can get as many as we want; but the idea is that those who volunteer first shall be compelled to serve only for one year, after which others may be substituted. It is all very well to talk about putting on regulations ; but the great difficulty in this country, as in every other, is to get men to

volunteer, and we have to be careful in that respect. This has been the law for a long time.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 79-Army Act, &c., to apply to active service-

I propose to insert after the words ' United Kingdom ' iD the second line the words 1 the King's regulations.' In the first draft of the Bill these words were omitted, but the officers in my department advised very strongly that we should continue to use the King's regulations, and I thought the reasons they gave were very strong. These regulations are the result of many years' experience.

I think this is not the same as the old Act. I object most emphatically to placing the officers or men of the militia force of this country under any disability as citizens. This clause makes every officer and man of the militia subject to this superior officer, ' while upon or within any rifle range or any armoury.' Do the words, ' while in the uniform of his corps,' apply to all these clauses, or do they not ? A man might happen to be on a rifle range or in an armoury on civilian business.
That means in uniform.

If it does, all right; but we have to teach the officers and politicians of the country that the officers and men of our militia are not to be subjected to the militarism of Europe or the United States. I believe the United States' regular army system is the most tyrannical in the world. We all know what the military systems of Germany, France and Russia are, with respect to the tyr-rany of officers. In England it is bad enough, but England in that respect is free and liberal' compared with any other nation in the world. We do not want to engraft on the Canadian militia a system that will put any officer, or man under any disability as a citizen. Why should any officer commanding a regiment or a company, when off duty, want to have the slightest control over any man under him ? If he cannot command the respect of his men without having this law at his back, he ought to get out of the force. Of course if he should be on duty or in uniform, the case would be different.

It is very doubtful if this clause would not apply even while the [DOT]man was not on duty. We should have it well understood that a man has a right to say anything he pleases to an officer, provided he is not under him or on duty at the time.

Once drill is over, the officer should not have any control over
the men under military regulations. Jit is a disgrace that in Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto our militia officers are afraid to express an opinion. They will tell you, I am only a lieutenant in some tuppeny-ha'-penny regiment
Order.

In the permanent corps of course men cannot express their opinion, but there are officers in our volunteer regiments in the cities and towns who dare not call their souls their own, who dare not express an opinion even on the Militia Act, because they happen to be only a lieutenant or a captain.
A provisional lieutenant.
No, the provisional fellows talk sometimes.
Why not strike out the woi'd ' also ' and substitute the word ' or ' ?

Better add a subsection. I know that this has been used by senior officers to make the juniors believe they have control over them. A man who can command respectable men in no other way than this should not wear the uniform.
Will my hon. friend draft a clause ?
Under .what dis-t cipline are the men of the militia while on active service ? For instance, in the case of mutiny, what Act would apply ?
Our own regulations supplemented by the imperial regulations wherever ours are found wanting.

I am not speaking of regulations, but of the Act. In the case I have mentioned, would the English Mutiny Act apply ? That Act is re-enacted from year to year. It is brought into force by this section.
The Army Act is what it is called, and although it is re-enacted every year, that is only a form.

It is a little more than a form, because parliament is at liberty not to re-enact it.
On section S3-provision for families of men killed, &c.
I move that this be amended by inserting the words ' On active service ' after the word ' killed.'

Are troops engaged at the rifle range counted as being on active service, drill or training, or on duty ? If a man is wounded while engaged on a rifle range, is he counted as being wounded as being on duty, or not ? For this brings up


the broad question we had before us in discussing section 68.
If my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) will look at the interpretation clause-No. 2-he will find these expressions defined.
I infer that a man attending at a rifle range is not on duty ?
No.

The interpretation clause defines ' on active service ' as applying to those enrolled, enlisted, drafted or warned for service or duty during an emergency, or when he is on duty or when he has been warned for duty in aid of the civil power. That appears to me rather complicated.
Suppose that an officer is taking a course of equitation and he is killed, is he counted as having been killed on duty ?
I think not.
It has been ruled that he is not. An officer in Halifax was killed under these circumstances. I always claimed that that officer was killed while on duty.
He was not at the school, but was drilling at his own house.

That does not make any difference. Drilling should not be confined to the school, but if men will take an interest and perfect themselves in drill at their own places-however, we need not discuss the question now.

The case referred to is that of Major Maxwell. He was killed by being thrown from his horse. I always thought that something should have been done for his widow. It is well enough to say that the general regulations apply only thus or so, but the case was one in which something should have been done.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) brought up the ease and my recollection is that we voted a gratuity.
I think not.

I certainly did not notice any item of that kind in any estimates that were voted. I did not know the man or anything about him except what I learned of the circumstances of his death. As I understand the facts, he was attending the military school. Whether he was in barracks or not makes no difference ; he was under military law' from the time he entered the school until he would have left it- until he did leave it, for he was in attendance at the time of his death. I have always felt that the claims of his family Mr. DANIEL.
should have been recognized under the statute.
Mr. "FOWLER.	It seems to me that
' drill or training or on duty ' would cover such a case. It does not make any difference w'hether he gets his meals at barracks or at his own home. If he were on his wTay to the school his case would come within Ibis section. Of course, if he were taking a ride for exercise that would be another matter. But if he were on his way to or from the school at the time the accident happened, I would think his representatives should have the benefit of this section,- just as a volunteer is held to be under orders from the time he starts for the annual drill until he returns to his home.

I looked into the case very carefully some years ago, but I am not certain whether I recall the facts accurately. I went into the case from a sympathetic point of view, because I was very anxious to take favourable action. My impression is that the report of the District Officer Commanding w'as that Major Maxwell did not come within the meaning of the section. He was mounting his horse to go for a ride but not to go to the school.
Mr, FOWLER. That is not the case I have in mind, but the case of one who was in attendance upon, including going to or returning from the school of equitation.'

That would be different.

This only requires persons to place these things at the disposal of the department ; I think it ought to give the department the right to take possession of them.
The Crown has that right.

Some time ago I drew the minister's attention to the omission of the words ' horse and wagon ' belonging to a farmer, as these things are likely to be called into requisition oftener than railways and steamships.

This part of the Act is copied from the Imperial Statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 13 goes a little further, it practically authorizes taking possession. The last words of the first paragraph say :
And may also impress any horses, mules, oxen or other animals required for military purposes.

30&DEN. This does not seem to me to be exactly intended to meet the case provided for in section 13. exists and where you make a requisition, you are entitled to have that requisition complied with under a penalty upon the person refusing. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would require to be amended to cover that.
That the section be amended by inserting in the fourteenth line after the word ' vessel ' the word's ' wagon, carriage or pack animal.'

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Surely if an officer made a return representing a man to be present who was not present and received pay for him, it would be a distinct case of f o lse representation, and he would be amenable under the Criminal Code.
It is not only the case of a man who is not there, but the case of a man who is there and who is enrolled in another corps.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He cannot be present in two places at the same time unless he is an Irishman or a bird.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Criminal Code would cover any misrepresentation as to the number of horses.

Is there in the Criminal Code any special punishment provided for false pretenses ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes. But there seems to be a provision here for making a man guilty of an indictable offence, but without providing any penalty.

I should imagine that these clauses were originally drafted before the Criminal Code was revised. Otherwise, you may have confusion by making provision in this statute lor matters already covered to a certain extent by the Crimianl Code or the English Army Act.

Section agreed to.
Sections from 100 to 107 agreed to.
On section 108-refusal to attend drill.
Mr. DANIEiL. I have in my hand several suggestions sent me by an officer who has had a good deal of experience in the militia. He suggests that at the end of this section the following should be added :
And the regimental orders o£ the corps properly issued and promulgated during the time of the annual drill or training shall he sufficient notice to such officers or men to attend.

On section 112,
Every person who unlawfully disposes of or removes any arms, accoutrements or other articles belonging to the Crown or corps, or who refuses to deliver them up when lawfully required, or has them in his possession, except for lawful cause, the proof of which shall lie upon him, shall incur a penalty of twenty dollars for each offence ; but nothing in this section shall prevent such offender from being indicted and punished for any greater offence, if the facts amount to such greater offence : and such offender may he arrested by order of the justice of the peace before whom the complaint is made, upon affidavit showing that there is reason to believe that such offender is about to leave Canada, carrying with him any such arms, accoutrements or articles.

My military friend suggests that at the end of that clause we should add the words :
Or if he have neglected or refused to deliver or return such articles after being properly notified or required so to do.
The clause in the present Bill has been found to work admirably for some thirty or forty years.
The fact that these regulations have been in existence thirty or forty years without change is, I think, one of the reasons why my friend makes the suggestion lie does.
I should be very glad if my hon. friend will send me a copy of the proposed amendment, as we might take it up, if necessary, on the third reading.

It is covered by section 112.
On section 113-refusal to aid the civil power.

In copying this clause some words were omitted, and I simply wish to restore them, making the clause read the same as the clause of the existing Act. I move to insert, after the word ' penalty,' the words ' in an officer, not exceeding one hundred dollars, and if a man.'

I do not object to the amendment. I presume that the other section referring to the troops called out to aid the civil power will come up to-morrow. I would call the minister's attention to one point now, so that he may think it over. I think it would be in harmony with the spirit of the times and with the wish of the people that there should be a clause providing that when the militia are called out to aid the civil power, the pay of the men shall be at least equal to that which it would be necessary to pay to special constables. These towns, rather than go to the expense of hiring special constables, call out the militia-the poor soldier has to serve them at 50 cents a day.

I suppose we would have to fix the amount.
