On section 36,
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN moved that the section be struck out and that the following be inserted in lieu thereof :
The district officer commanding, if he is present in the locality and able to act, or if he is not so present, or from! sickness or other cause is unable to act, the senior officer of the active militia in any locality, shall call out the same or any portion thereof, as he considers necessary for the purpose of preventing or suppressing any such actual or anticipated riot or disturbance, when thereunto required in -writing by the chairman or custos of the quarter sessions of the peace, or by any three justices of the peace, of whom the warden, mayor or other head or acting head of the municipality or county in [DOT]which such riot or disturbance occurs or is anticipated as aforesaid, shall be one, unless he has declined or is unable to act, which fact shall in that case be set forth in the requisition, and shall not be open to dispute by the officer upon whom the requisition is made : provided always that the permanent force, if, in the opinion of the officer upon whom the 'requisition is made, a sufficient number of that force is available, is to be employed upon this duty, before resort is had to other mill-tia corps.
This section was drafted by the Department of Justice the officers of that department having carefully read the criticisms which were made here when this Bill was discussed in committee before.

I think this clause is a much better one than the old one. Wherever I a permanent force is available, I think i should always be brought out, In case of riot or anticipated riot, in preference to the militia of the town, As we all know, the militia might be compelled to act against their own friends and companions. So that I think the provision is a very good one.

When this question was discussed on a previous occasion, the general feeling seemed to be that some measures should be taken to prevent the militia being called out before the civil power was exhausted. Our experience in recent years has shown that the militia have been called out before the civil power has been taxed to its full extent. I would like to know whether the Minister of Militia thinks that there is in this clause sufficient safeguard against any such abuse. It was suggested that we should put upon the municipal authorities the duty of engaging special constables, and only calling on the militia when such precaution proved ineffective. Take the case down at Sydney, there is much dispute as to whether there was any necessity for bringing the militia to quell the labour troubles down there, and I believe the municipality has repudiated the action of the justices of the peace who sent the requisition for military aid.

I cannot see very well what greater obstacle you can provide against the unnecessary calling out of the troops than compelling the municipality interested to pay the cost. When the municipalities have to pay, they will be very careful about calling out the militia.

Is it not a fact that they generally refuse to pay ?
Sir FREDERICK BORDEiN. No.

There are two points that occur to me in connection with this section. In the first line I would suggest that we substitute the word ' district ' for the word * locality,' because no one could tell what ' locality ' means in this section.
That is the present law.

But we are trying to amend it. However, if the committee thinks that the language is clear enough, 1 shall not make a motion. But there is something at the end : ' provided always, that the permanent force is not available and in sufficient numbers for the purpose.' This could be construed to mean that, if in the opinion of the district officer commanding, the permanent force is not available in sufficient numbers, then the non-permanent militia should be called out. To my mind, what is intended is that the non-permanent militia should be called out to supplement the permanent force in case the later is not sufficient in numbers. In the discussion we had on this clause the general opinion was that the permanent force should be resorted to whenever possible.

I think the objection of the hon. member for Haldimand is well taken. We should make it perfectly clear that the permanent force IS to be . called out to the extent to which it is available, and that only in the event of that force being insufficient should we call on the militia, and then only call on the militia to supplement the permanent force. That evidently is the intention, but we should see that it is clearly expressed.

It would be rather dangerous to make the law too strin-gefft. It might be advisable, for instance, not to call out the Permanent Force, but to hold it in reserve for some other duty, and no one is in a better position to judge of the circumstances than the district or senior officer, who is on the spot. We must give him gome discretion in the matter.

I would suggest that we amend the clause by striking out the words ' in the opinion of the officer,' and substitute the words ' so far as it is available.' The clause would then read : ' Provided always, that the permanent force, so far as it is available, is to be employed upon this duty before calling on the militia.' My own opinion is that the militia should be
called on first. I think that every locality should be taught to keep its own law and order. I believe in self-governing communities, and I do not believe in this system of calling in the militia from Quebec to go to Sydney or from Toronto to Sault Ste. Marie. That is one reason why I want the pay of the militia increased to that of special constables. That would teach the municipalities a lesson. I am told that the Sault disturbance could have been quelled by one good, sensible man acting in proper time, and nine out of ten of these disturbances, to quell which the troops are called out, could have been settled without having resort to that extreme measure.	.

I would like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Justice in connection with this clause. You will see that the district officer commanding, very properly, has no power to refuse a requisition that is made upon 'him. And the clause goes on to provide that the requisition shall be in writing by the chairman of the quarter sessions, or by any three justices of the peace, of whom the warden, mayor, or other head of the muni-cipaliiy shall be one ; and if the mayor, warden or other head refuses to act. then the requisition is to state such refusal, and one other justice of the peace has to take his place. You will see that the warden or mayor is the only one of these three who is responsible to the municipality as regards expenditure. It seems to me, therefore, it would be a proper thing to provide that, if the mayor refuses to sign this requisition the signature of two other justices of the peace-that is, four justices of the peace altogether-should be required. It v ould be necessary to make the section read something in this manner :
-or by any three justices of the peace of whom the warden, mayor or other head or acting head of the municipality or county in which such riot or disturbance occurs or is anticipated as aforesaid, shall be one, but, if he declines or is unable to act, then, by four justices of the peace.
It is pretty well understood that in many instances justices of the peace are too quick perhaps, to call upon the district officer commanding for assistance before the resources of the municipality are exhausted. That is the experience. Certainly, it was fihe experience in Vallevfield, I think it was the experience three years ago in British Columbia, and I doubt if it is not the ex perience in Sydney at the present time. This amendment gives a little more protection to the municipality which after alt must foot the bill.
Section as amended, agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

' These are therefore to require you to call out the active militia at present in '-they are in the locality.
In the district.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The permanent force is a part of the active militia, and when requisition is made upon the district officer cOvinmanding he must consult the statute under which he is to act, and the statute says that the part of the militia which is first to be called upon is the permanent force. He has to read the statute in order to ascertain what his powers are, and he will find that the permanent force are first to be called upon, if they are available in sufficient number.
At all events, these words do not make any reference to the permanent force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The permanent force is a part of the active militia, and the active militia includes the permanent force.

At the present moment a Quebec permanent corps are in Mi PUI TEE.
Sydney, Cape Breton, some hundreds of miles away.	.
Is it the intention that in case the permanent force are called out they are to be paid for by the government or by the municipality ?
By the municipality.
Why should their cost be a fine upon the municipality ? It may not be the fault of the municipality that this riot occurs, and I think they should be paid out of the general revenue of the country.
I think if that were so, every time a person got disorderly in the streets the permanent corps would be gent for.

Would it not be better to alter that requisition in this way :
These are therefore to require you to call out the active militia in the district.
Instead of saying as at present in any particular place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then that would mean that we have no permanent corps.
If there are any permanent corps in the district, then they would be available in accordance with the terms of section 36.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But if there are not ?
The active militia covers both, it seems to me.
It seems to me a serious matter that the town of Sydney should have to bear the expense of taking the permanent force from Quebec to Sydney.
They deposited the money in the bank before the force started, $10,000.
I saw somewhere that the town of Sydney had notified the militia authorities that they would not pay a cent of this.
They did not. Before we allowed the troops to start the money was put in the bank.

I think the government cannot be too emphatic in impressing upon these municipalities that they must preserve law and order in their own community. I object to the ratepayers of Victoria county being called upon to pay one dollar of the cost of sending the permanent force to suppress riots in any part of Canada.

When the militia are called out by three magistrates. I do not see why the municipalities should have to

pay the cost. I think whenever a riot occurs and it becomes necessary to call out the militia-ancl they can only he called out by three magistrates-the government ought to be in some measure responsible for their expense. The militia are a government force, and it is unfair to compel the municipality to pay the expenses of the militia so called out. The magistrates are responsible to the town, or perhaps responsible to the county, they are competent judges of the necessity of outside aid, and I do not think it is fair that a little municipality should be called upon to pay the entire expense.
Why should the Dominion treasury be made liable ?

Because the militia are under the control of the Dominion government, under the control of the Minister of Militia as a member of the government, and if they are to go at all, they should go at the expense of the Dominion government.

Each province or subdivision of a province is responsible for maintaining law and order, and it is only in extraordinary occasions, cases of emergency, that this power should be exercised by the local authorities in calling upon the central power for aid. I aja'ee with the hon. member from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) absolutely, that municipalities should be discouraged as far as possible from exercising a power which is only meant to be available in an emergency. We should not offer too many invitations or too many facilities for having recourse to that power. I may point out that at the pre(-sent time, the militia are being used to perform police duty in suppressing a street row in the city of London. I object emphatically to any ratepayer of Victoria county, or of any other county in the Dominion of Canada, being called upon to pay police expenses, even though the Dominion troops are being used, or to pay one farthing of the expenses of suppressing a riot.

It is the law abiding citizens in all cases who have to pay the cost of suppressing disturbances on the part of the citizens who are not law abiding. It seems to me that if the people of this country pay taxes to support this permanent force, they have a right to their services to suppress serious local riots.
Not as a police force.

To maintain law and order within the boundaries of Canada as well as to resist invasion. You have authority to call upon this force in case of emergency. Here is an emergency ; by this very Act you define an emergency to be a riot and insurrection beyond the power of the local police force to suppress. It does seem to m# that in case the permanent force
are called out the expenses should not be saddled upon the municipality.

It is only when a local disturbance becomes a riot and the law of the country is set at defiance that the federal authority is called in. Therefore it is when t'he local police in the country break down that the militia come in. Under the general idea that the government must preserve law and order in the country when the authority of the local municipality breaks down this government should pay tor the suppression of any disturbance. But unfortunately this was settled at a time when the province of Ontario was settling everything on a very narrow basis. If the province of Nova Scotia wanted a wharf t'hey required that we should pay half the cost of it.
We pay all the cost now.

I agree with my hon. friend from East Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour) because he struck the proper key and stated a sound principle both in morals and equity when he said that if the law makes it legal for the municipality, or some officials in the municipality, to call out the militia the charge should be upon the country as a whole, because the public law of t'he land is evoked and the local authority 'is in abeyance.

When this matter was introduced first I took the ground that the militia force should not be called out for police purposes to put down a riot in a scrub town in w-hich the municipality do not know how to preserve law and order.
I object to my hon. friend referring in so disagreeable a manner to Lindsay.

We are a law abiding people there and do not require to call out the militia to keep us in order. I repeat most emphatically that no militiaman' ought to be called out to do police duty at 50 cents a day to be insulted and spat upon especially w'hen he is not in a position to arrest a man for disorderly conduct. The law should be so amended that if these men are called out they should be called out as policemen, given $2.50 a day and have the power to step out of the ranks and arrest a man if he is disorderly. I want to convert my hon. friend here. Nine out of ten of these riots are caused through some action on the part of local people, nine out of ten of these riots are caused by the residents becoming disorderly, they are the people Who encourage a riot and I say that no one outside of the municipality should be called upon to pay a farfihing of the expense of putting down a riot in that municipality.
The difficulty Is that under the law two or three magistrates who are not responsible to the municipality can put a large expense upon the municipality.

That is the municipality's own fault.
Mr.- FOWLER. How is it the municipality's own fault? They have no control over the magistrates. My hon. friend says that it is the fault of the municipality. Not at all. If you. give the power to the municipal council w'ho are responsible to the people, then it might be all right to make the municipality pay for it, but you allow irresponsible persons, and magistrates are not always responsible persons, to perform this duty and saddle the municipality with the cost.

The municipal council in Sydney is composed of as able men as those composing any municipal council in this Dominion. The citizens of Sydney are as orderly as those of any city in the Dominion. A company has been formed there and a foreign element has been brought into the place.
Not Highland Scotch ?

They are not Scotch. The Scotch know how to behave themselves in whatever part of the world they are placed. Even amongst savages they know how to behave themselves. But, that is outside of the question altogether. Here vou have a body of regulars down at Quebec. They are doing nothing, they have nothing to do because the cities of Quebec are orderly in every respect, and these regulars are sent down to Sydney to preserve order there. If their travelling expenses in going down and coming home are paid that is as much as could be expected by the municipality of Sydney.

Those who are instrumental in the first instance in having the soldiers called out may have been the original cause of all the friction. A foreign element is brought in by parties who are engaged in carrying on a work. Ihej are brought in to serve these parties own interests in the first instance and because these men object to their being handled to the liking of the company, friction arises, the militia are called out and the country has to pay for it If the militia are cailed out let the municipality pay for them and when the municipality knows that they are responsible for the cost of bringing the militia in they will remove the cause of friction. I would be very sorry to support a proposition that the country as a whole should pay the expenses in connection with a matter of this kind. I think the bon. minister is quite right when he makes the law read as he proposes to do.

The main object of the permanent force is defined in section 30 of this Bill wlien it says :
The permanent force shall furnish schools of instruction for the ipilitia, and provide instructors therefor ;-
The hon. member for Victoria, Nova Scotia (Mr. Ross)
Read the rest of it.

It has other functions, but I said this was the main one.
-and it shall also be available, at all times, for general service.
The general service referred to there is something more serious than putting down riots. When any hon. member of this House says that this corps is idling all the time and that it might as well be employed tor the suppression of rioting, I think he entirely overlooks the fact that it is doing important work in instructing the balance of the force, and that this is the principal reason for its existence. It does seem to me that if this force which has been established mainly for the instruction of t'he balance, or the larger part of the force is removed from its instructional duties, that balance of the force is therefore losing its teaching in consequence, and it is only right that the government should receive pay from the municipality. It does seem absurd. I think, to charge this to the whole of Canada.	[DOT]	.

It does not seem that t'he hon. minister has answered the objection of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Daniel). I would like to have him state whether it is not possible to alter this requisition so as to make it more conformable with section 36. It seems to me that seme slight change was made there. There seems to be a portion that cannot be very well altered, but if the hon. minister would alter that provision so as to refer to thq active militia in the district, I think it would answer t'he objection of my hon. friend from St. John.

The language used is that which exists in the present law. It has been found to work very well and I suppose it was followed by the draftsman who prepared this clause. One hesitates to depart from a phrase or from language which has been used for many years and which is found to work well.
But the hon. minister must not forget that section 36 has been altered and it is only to make this requisition conform with the alteration that my hon. friend from St. John proposes the change.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If you insert the word ' district,' the permanent force could not go to the city of Halifax to suppress a

riot, because there is no permanent force in Nova Scotia. It is better to allow these elastic words to be used ; you have to trust to the discretion and good judgment of somebody, and it is better to leave that to the discretion of the district officer commanding.
The whole Dominion is divided into military districts, and there is a permanent corps in each district.
Not in Nova Scotia.

Even so, I do not see what objection there can be, because the words [DOT] active militia ' do not refer to the permanent corps if there is no permanent corps in that district. I am sure the Minister of Justice could suggest a wording of the clause that would meet the case.
I cannot see any objection to that word ' district.'
Instead of allowing the militia to be called out by three magistrates', why not say that it shall be done by a majority of the municipal council ?

That might take too long.
Mr. MAC-LEAN. They might refuse to make a quorum.

When the original Act provided that three magistrates might call out the militia, we had no county or municipal .councils in the greater part of the Dominion. At that time the magistrates were members of the sessions, and they had the authority that is now vested in municipal bodies. In moulding our Act to-day. we should give recognition to the representative institutions as we find them : and, as the magistrates have ceased to have any civil authority, we should substitute for the three magistrates of the old law the mayor and two or three municipal councillors, who can just as readily be gotten at as three magistrates.

Apparently the sentiment of this committee is against the indiscriminate employment of the militia to aid the civil power ; and, that being so, it seems to me that it would be better to have the municipal council called together, or that a majority of the municipal council should sign the requisition to call out the militia. If you allow it to be done by three magistrates who are not responsible in any way to the people, the militia could very easily be called out when the occasion was not serious enough to demand it.

My own opinion is that the militia should not be called out for
this purpose at all. Instead of ordering the boys out and paying them 50 cents a day, let the municipal authorities swear them in as special constables and pay them $1.50 or $2 a day. When the militiaman stands there with his uniform and his rifle, every pup in the town can spit on him and he dare not leave the ranks, whereas if he were a special constable he could take that fellow by the scruff of the neck and put him in the lockup. The munclpal authorities ought to be taught the idea of providing for the peace and order of the municipalities, and pay for it.

Although I am not a militiaman. I will venture to say a word on this question. The suggestion has been made that the militia should only be called out by a majority of the municipal council, tut I would point out that in many districts of the province of British Columbia there are no municipalities, and consequently the militia could not be called out at all under such a law. For instance, on the Skeena river, where a strike is feared, there are no municipalities, and so the justices of the peace must be the authority to take action in such a contingency. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) that the machinery for calling out the militia should not be made too easily available, and further, that when the militia is called out in aid of the" civil power, the municipalities should be made to understand that they must pay for it. If the government were to pay the militia every time they were called out for such duty, then the militia would be at the beck and call of every person in the country, but if the municipality is obliged to pay it is a very great safeguard. Let me say that I am very strongly apposed to the militia being called out to suppress riots in towns where the members of the militia force themselves reside, because sometimes they are called upon to act against their personal friends, and that is a condition that should be avoided if possible. I repeat that in the province of British Columbia, where there are no municipalities, the power to call out the militia must be in the hands of the justices of the peace.

The more we discuss this matter the more apparent it becomes that the body representative of the people who pay the cost should have the authority to say when the militia shall be called out. In provinces where municipal councils are incorporated you could say that the mayor and three of the town council-I do not think a majority of the council is necessary -should have the power to call the militia out, and as these gentlemen know they have to pay the cost they will be rather chary about exercising the power except in case of great stress. I think that would solve the whole difficulty. If you leave it to three magistrates, a big company like the Steel Company at Sydney could easily pick up three magistrates and get them to call out

the militia, whether it was right to do so or not. X am not speaking of magistrates as a whole, hut a company like the Steel Company might have three or four magistrates in its employ; whereas if it had to go to the city or town council, which had to pay the bill, it would meet with a different order of things. I deprecate the calling out of the militia on all occasions, and I think that would be the better plan to adopt.

Let me say to my hon. friend that although this law has been in force for forty years, there has never been a ease in my knowledge-and 1 have looked over the cases carefully- where it has been abused. The law has worked well for forty years, and 1 think before that in the old provinces of Upper and Lower Canada, and why not leave it alone ? I might point out one ease on the other side, the case of Valleyfleld, where the mayor absolutely refused to act. Will any one say that it was not necessary on that occasion to take the action that was taken '! I think not ; and yet under the proposal of my hon. friend, it would be impossible to get the aid of the militia in similar conditions. The law has worked well ; why not leave it alone ?
In the case of Val-leyfield, could not the civil authorities have sworn in enough special constables to have preserved order without calling out the militia, if they had not found it easy to do so ?

What is the meaning of the word ' municipality ' as used in this section ? We have a county municipality, which embraces incorporated villages, towns-ships and towns, each and every one of which is a municipality. Would you seek to recover pay from an incorporated village, or from the county ? I am inclined to think it would be from the county as the language stands here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would be from the particular municipality directly charged with the maintenance of peace within the district where the riot occurs. These occurrences never take place in the country parts. This legislation is designed to meet actual cases that arise, not imaginary cases that have not arisen and are not likely to arise. Outside of the case at Valleyfield. no such emergency has arisen in the province of Quebec outside of a town or city, and I am sure the same thing would apply to Ontario.

But in the event of your endeavouring to recover from the municipality the cost of the militia being called out, would it not be as well to define what is meant by the municipality- whether it is meant to be the county or one of the local municipalities, such as the village, town or township ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Has not a city, a town or a village a separate municipal existence from a county in Ontario ?
Not entirely. Cities have, towns may not have, villages and townships do not have. They have to pay their statute taxes to the counties, and they are controlled in that measure by the counties.

It strikes me that you are violating the principle of no taxation without representation when you allow these magistrates to call out the militia. I am surprised that the hon. member for La-belle, who is a stickler for constitutional liberty, has not seen this point, and come to the assistance of those who are fighting for constitutional principles.
My hon. friend is doing it better than I could.

In the event of a* vacancy in the office of iGeneral Officer Commanding, or in the absence of that officer from Canada, the command of the militia shall devolve upon the next senior combatant officer on the HeadQuarters Staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Somebody must act under him. He will not go out and take care of the militia himself. He must appoint somebody to take his place.

I do not object to the amendment especially but I might aS well discuss the point which I am about to mention here. I may illustrate what I mean by taking England as an example. I want to know if it is the intention of the hon. minister to bring about an interchange in the headquarters staff along these hues. At the present time the headquarters staff are fixtures.
No, they only hold office for five years.
There never was a change in any of them.
There will be.

In England after a man spends a few years on the headquarters staff he is sent out to his regiment, or brigade, or division in order to get sharpened up in his duties in the service. In other words, being office men for a term of years, they get rusty in their work. Is it the hon. minister's intention to carry out that system ?

Yes, already we have passed a regulation limiting the term to five years. That was passed three years ago. I would be inclined to follow the English rule limiting it to four vears, and before an officer could return to the headquarters staff again, make it necessary that he should serve a year in some of the districts or in England in the way of exchange. Not only that, but I propose in the regulations to require after a certain numbei; of years that every officer on the Headquarters Staff shall have passed through the English Staff College. An arrangement has been made whereby two officers of the militia of Canada are permitted to attend the Staff College every year, and it is very obvious that at the end of four or five years we shall have a considerable number of officers, if advantage is taken of this opportunity, possessing the qualifications which are considered essential to the performance of staff duties of this kind.
Is there any intention, having regard to the fact that there will be an interchange of officers, to bring about a gradual infusion of the two forces ?
Yes.
I am glad of that.

That is one of the things that was discussed at the meeting of the defence committee which I had the honour of attending, and it was agreed that so soon as Canadian officers were technically qualified by active service or by being graduates of the Staff College, an exchange would take place. It was agreed that if an imperial officer were re-

quired in this country, or if we saw fit to ask for an imperial officer for instance to take charge of the Royal Military College, we should get a quid pro quo, we should have the privilege of sending the same number of officers over to serve in the imperial army.
Of course the minister has the full authority of his government witli that regard.
Yes.

That being the case r shall not take up time drawing attention to some interesting pictures in the Montreal * Herald.' There is an editorial in that paper whic*b I am sorry to have to place on the records of the House, but it will show the absurdity of the minister of war. Tlie organ of the Minister of Agriculture who is the minister of war at times, and superintendent general of the whole business says :
The Canadian militiaman is eager to learn something of actual use during his short time of learning, and in his search for that he is apt to neglect the niceties of military etiquette to such an extent that British officers are horrified at his lackness in saluting according to the regulations of the drill book.
We are told that the Minister of Agriculture is most punctilious in his own department. I do not know how low he makes the civil servants bow to him, but they certainly must approach him in fear and tliem-bling. They require to stand some distance from him, especially if they happen to be bigger than he, and pay him all due homage. In one of these pictures the Minister of Militia 'is standing in front with his hat off showing that beautiful profile which we all admire so much, and a little to the right we find the Minister of Agriculture, or war, with his hat doffed returning a salute. In the next picture the Minister of Agriculture is standing in an easier position chatting with some officers. I shall not read the whole article as the minister has promised to carry out these interchanges with the imperial service. I assume that the Minister of Militia is taking up his position again, and that he has sent the Minister of Agriculture to look after the hens and the eggs. I am informed that it has appeared 'in the newspapers that amongst the officers this gentleman was instrumental in forcing on the 13th Scottish Light Dragoons, two of them are no credit to anybody. One of them came into the Laprairie camp with a pair of gaiters and a little spur screwed into the heel of the gaiter so that he could not ride, and be had two swords, one on his right and one on his left and one splendid black eye. He remained in camp long enough to make an exhibition of himself and then he was returned home. I may be wrong but I under-208J
stand that these are the facts. T'hese are two of the men that the Minister of Agriculture held up the Scottish Light Dragoons to appoint, and as a result of which we have lost the best General Officer Commanding that ever stood on Canadian soil. One of his officers came into camp with a sword on each side, a little spur fastened into a heel of a pair of gaiters and a black eye ; the other was not very long in camp before he was hauled up before the police court and fined $20.

On section 6 (a).
The Governor in Council may appoint a Militia Council to advise the minister on all matters relating to the militia, which may be referred to the Council by the minister. The composition, procedure and powers of the council shall he as prescribed
Mr
WARD. What does that mean ?

It is proposed to adopt the system which has been adopted in England, as a result of the report of the commission which is known as the Esher Commission, composed of Lord Esher, Admiral Sir John Fisher and General Clarke. The council, which is called the Army Council in England, we propose to call the Militia Council. In England the Secretary of State for War is the chairman.
Formerly the English militia were not under the Secretary of State for War, but were under the Secretary of State for Home Affairs.

For the last ten years it has been under the Secretary of State for War. On the Army Council there are four military members called, respectively, the first military member, the second military member, the third military member and the fourth military member. The first military member has charge of military policy in all its branches, war staff duties, intelligence, mobilization, plans of operations, training, military history, war regulations ; he is chief of the general stuff. The second military member will be the ad-
Who is that officer in England ?
The financial secretary is a permanent office:'. The parliamentary Under Secretary is the fust civil member.
That is not the permanent Under Secretary ?

No, the permanent Under Secretary is the secretary of the commission. In England there is no deputy minister, and the financial officer of the department corresponds to our deputy minister. We are not in a position to follow the English system exactly ; but the Minister of Militia as chairman, and the four military members will correspond exactly with the similar members on the English board. The chief staff officer-
There is no chief staff officer now.
No. but we propose to have one, and I am taking a vote for that purpose.
Would the duties of our quartermaster-general correspond with those of the English quartermaster-general ?

To a large extent. It is difficult for me to explain, in as great detail as I would like to do, the scheme, because we have not yet been able to get the regulations. I do not know that they are yet completed. Sir Edward Ward, with whom I have been in correspondence, very kindly offered to send them to me as soon as they were published : but in the meantime I can only give such information as I have been able to get from reports which I have read in the newspapers, and correspondence which I have had with some eminent military authorities there.
I understand that the chief staff officer will largely have control of the militia ?
Operations, intelligence, and so on.
Would he be interfered with by any of the civil officers ?

No. Each man has his own department to himself. But they will discuss matters as a council, the Minister of Militia being in the chair, and having the advantage of these officers face to face in his presence discussing all important matters affecting the welfare of tlie militia. Perhaps I am too enthusiastic, but it Seems to me that the adoption of this system will be the dawn of better days for the militia. I believe it must result in the different branches of the militia being in very much better touch with each other than ever before. It will result in the minister at least having the opportunity of be-, coming acquainted with every branch of his department, and it will result in continuity in the service which we have never had in this country. Each conclusion at which this council may arrive will be a matter of record, so that each minister will have the opportunity of seeing in writing the results of the conferences which took place previous to his coming, and the reasons underlying the different policies adopted from time to time.

In Britain I have every reason to believe that this committee or council will work well. The matter was agitated for a long time, and there was a series of very able articles in the Ron don * Times,' written by its editor. Mr. Amery, who wrote a history of the South African troubles. Mr. Amery educated the public along these lines very thoroughly, and I an; satisfied that the scheme will work well there. I do not see any reason why a similar scheme should not work well here, provided the council be composed of men of independence of character. Of course, it will be said that men can be had in Canada equally as independent as you can find in England, but we must not shut our eyes to the fact that many of the officers occupying the highest positions in England are men of wealth and in a better position to talk straight to the government than would be the officers employed in the civil service here. One reason I have urged against any officer of a Dominion force being under the Army Act is that it prevents his giving that free expression to his views which we should encourage in our men. While I occupied the position of command in my regiment I always encouraged every officer under me to give expression to his views, even when they were critical of my own policy, but talk in confidence to members of the force and they will tell you that they dare not say a word. I say to'the minister, wipe away all these restrictions, wipe away this Army Act in so far as it applies to our men, and let our officers approach him like men and give both him and the public the benefit of their views. I had a long letter sent me from Kingston the other day complaining of some officer in the military college for having expressed sympathy with Russia, and asking me to
bring the matter up in the House. Why, I commend that officer. He was not talking to his cadets, but was on his holidays, and he had a perfect right to express his opinion on the Russian and Japanese war. And to say that because he happens to side with Russia we should drive him out of the position of professor in the military college is utterly absurd. So long as he does not talk this sort of thing to his cadets, no one can have anything to say to him.' He has a perfect right to express his own opinions outside the college, just as any man should have connected with the militia. The minister need not be afraid to trust the officers of the permanent force. He will do the country a service if he will wipe out from the statute-book all these restrictive resolutions, and tell the officers of the permanent force that they are at liberty to express their views on any question. If he will only encourage the members of the council to be independent and fearless, he will benefit the service, but if they are to be only timeservers the service will suffer.
Under the King's regulations the utmost possible independence wall be given each member of the council.

The minister has brought the headquarters staff under the Army Act. Go around and talk to these gentlemen, and they will tell you they dare not say a word. I would rather encourage them to come out like free men and do iiway with the dark-ages tyranny of Germany, France, the United States and other countries.

The question of military rank is to be allowed to remain in abeyance, and the members of the council will practically be in the position of Lords of the Admiralty, so that the highest possible freedom will be given them.
On section 68,
His Majesty shall be liable for compensation for injury to persons and for damage to property arising from the use of any rifle range under the control of the Department of Militia and Defence for target practice, carried on under regulations prescribed by this Act, provided that there shall be no claim for compensation for any injury due to negligence on the part of the person injured, or if such person, at the time the injury was sustained, was at the rifle range as a spectator of shooting, or in the case of injury to property where such injury was due to negligence on the part of the owner of the property.
The only criticism I would make upon this proposed section is with regard to the part referring to spectators. I do not see why a spectator injured by militiamen should not be compensated.
He would have his remedy under the civil law.
I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that the section does not provide for those who are using the range and receive injury.
Yes, that is provided for.

I have no objection to have any new draft made of my proposal, though, I must say, I do not think it exactly complimentary to the Department of . Justice that the Department of Militia should re-draft a clause which was prepared under the direction of the Department of Justice, without consulting the legal officers of the government. I still maintain the point I made this morning. These rifle ranges are organized by the government for the benefit of the militia or for the benefit of the country, according to the point of view you may take. They are managed under government regulation. The government allows people to go there-not only militiamen, or members of rifle clubs, but others-and practise shooting as long and as often as they like ; and the people who have properties alongside these ranges and who have certainly as much right to be on their own private property as these people have to be on the government property are liable to injury or death. Yet, because the people whose shooting causes the injury or death are not there under government regulation, the government will not hold itself responsible to give compensation. If the amendment is accepted as it has been re-drafted without the advice of the legal advisers of the government, the result will be that compensation will accrue only when injury is caused by shooting that is practised under government regulation. If, then, the government does not take the proper care to prevent people from being injured, there may be injuries for which there is no compensation. I have no objection to accept the amendment of the Minister of Militia, provided another clause is added which will make it imperative that the minister shall prevent shooting at the rifle ranges by others than those who shoot under the government regulation. Otherwise I cannot accept it. If my protest is not listened to, it will show what care the government have for those peaceful people who may be killed or injured on property alongside the rifle ranges. I think we pay enough for the militia that compensation should be provided for the case of people, possibly poor farmers, who are killed or injured as a result of this rifle practice. I am sorry to see that the militiamen seem to have adopted the habit of laughing at the farmers. Well, it may be that the farmers may resent their laughter as well as their bullets.

Why, the hon. gen tieman (Mr. Bourassa) takes that seriously. What is it that the hon. gentleman wants that is not already covered by the amend-Sir F. W. BORDEN.
ment that is proposed by the Minister of Militia ? Is the government to put a caretaker on each range to prevent pigeon shooters
Yes, if necessary.

Not at all. It would be perfectly absurd for the government to attempt to keep a man on every rifle range. And, in any case, why should the government be responsible for shooting by persons who have no right to be on the ranges ?
Mere trespassers.
Yes ; why should the government be responsible for injury done by such men, any more than it should be responsible for the accidental shooting of a man while out deer hunting ?

I do not see how this amendment of the minister covers such a case as that of Larose. I do not think it does cover it. In that case, I have reason to believe, the men were practising not under government regulation.
Yes.

I do not think so. It seems to me that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) is right. We ought to give full protection, and this section does not give it. The ranges have been removed from my constituency, but I am as much interested in the constituency where they now are. I do not think this amendment covers the cases at all. .

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is a very important question, and I think that perhaps, the committee would do well to take time to consider the purport of the amendment proposed. I think, for my part, that there is something in the observation of my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). We have erected these ranges-very properly so. They are made use of by the militia -very properly so. But we know that the modern rifle is a very dangerous instrument, and that great precaution should govern the use of it. The spirit of the amendment is that if the militia are practising rifle shooting and any casualty arises or any damage to property is occasioned, the government should be responsible. That is one of the responsibilities, I think, that the government should assume. But I understand that there are parties who go to shoot on these ranges quite irrespective of the militia. There may be a few of such men who go there and practice, which is a desirable thing in itself. But one hon. gentleman says that in such cases the government will not be responsible. 1 agree with him. But I say it is too serious a matter, and human life is too valuable, for anybody to be allowed to go on these ranges to shoot except under government regulations. If five or six young men want to go on the rifle range and shoot, it is quite pro-

per that they should do so ; but they should carry on their shooting under regulations of the government, and, if any casualty takes place, the government should be responsible.
That is exactly the amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand there is some difference of opinion as to whether the amendment which is proposed is sufficient to cover these contingencies. Under these circumstances, and as my hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) has done a good day's work, I would suggest that he should move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, and the Department of Justice should be asked to look into this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To draw an amendment, we must know what it is desired to effect by the amendment. If you create a rifle range and attract the public there for the purpose of practising rifle shooting, and the people do go there and use the rifle ranges in such a way as to cause injury to persons in the neighbourhood, I fail to see why there should not be responsibility upon the people who first established and who own the ranges. I do not see why we should stop half way. It seems to me it should be either one thing or the other-ei 1 her do not allow the rifle ranges to exist, or. if you allow them to exist, control them so that the public cannot be injured as a result of the use made of them.

I do not know whether the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) knows the nature of these things. He possibly has in mind a range like that down here at Rockeliffe. But nine-tenths of the rifle ranges in the country are vastly different from that. Going upon them you would not know that you were on a rifle range, unless you saw the flag flying or came across a little mound that the people had prepared at their own expense, with government assistance. Ranges are established by people at their own expense, with a little government assistance, and when these are taken over by the government they are just as much government ranges as any of these fancy ranges down here. When a man is injured in rifle shooting in one of these ranges, should not he be just as well treated as when he is injured in one of these headquarter ranges ? The men who were shooting on the Montreal range were city volunteers ; they had their flag flying, and they were practising.
We do not know whether they were practising under the regulations.

They had their flag flving, they had their markers there. They did not need to be in uniform at all, in fact they should not be in uniform. But this accident happened, and undoubtedly
the man was entitled to consideration, and I am surprised he did not get it. The reason was that some lawyer in Montreal adviseu him not to take the offer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The government was not responsible for it.

I remember well where a regiment was out rifle shooting, and bv accident they shot a cow which was peacefully grazing on the hills a mile or two in the rear, and the government had to pay for that cow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Supreme Court said the government was not bound to pay in the Montreal case.

On a technicality, the lawyers befuddled the case. There is a certain danger limit in the rear of all these rifle ranges, and if a man goes there knowing that he is in danger, he should run his own risk, and I do not think he is entitled to compensation if he gets hurt.

I think we might change slightly the amendment moved this afternoon by the hon. member for Labelle, to section 68. Where it reads, ' arising from the use of any rifle range, ' why not put in the words ' Under the control of the Department of Militia and Defence for target practice ? '

In order to make that section of any value you must have a clause defining what is meant by a rifle range under the control of the government. You would simply defeat every man who brought his action, from the fact that this rifle range was not a rifle range in the meaning of the law.

It appears to me it will be necessary to make it a criminal offence for a person who is unauthorized to use one of these rifle ranges ; otherwise I do not see how you can deal in a just and equitable way. As I understand this amendment, it will make the government liable for compensation to any one who receives injury from a rifle shot fired from the rifle range, whether the range has been authorized by the government or not. But there is nothing to allow the government to inflict a penalty on any one who shoots over that range without permission or authority. I do not see that you can proceed against the person who uses that range without authority, and I presume there are regulations forbidding any one to use a rifle range except those who are authorized by the regulations to do so.
I think we had better adopt the suggestion of the Prime Minister and let this matter stand over. Some members are absent who would like to discuss it.
I was anxious to get it settled.

I sjrmpathize with tlie Minister of Justice. I know that these gentlemen are after a remedy, and I sympathize with their object; but legally a remedy is no good unless you define it within strict terms ; otherwise you will entrap the suitor to bring an action, and you will defeat it by a technical objection. The headquarters of the rifle ranges dealt with in this Act are the headquarters of rifle ranges only ; you must have a section describing what a government range is, headquarters or no headquarters. That amendment as it stands now would not be worth a straw to anybody.

I would like to ask the minister if rifle clubs have a right to use those ranges ?
Mr. SAM,. HUGHES. Rifle clubs organized under the Act.
There are a number now who receive free ammunition, I understand.
They get assistance towards the construction of ranges.
Are injuries inflicted upon these rifle ranges, as well as injuries inflicted upon headquarters' rifle ranges provided for in this particular amendment ?
They are included if the shooting goes on under the regulations.
Does section 75 still stand in the Bill, providing that the cadet corps should be furnished with arms, ammunition and equipment under the conditions prescribed ?
Yes. that is there.

Take our high school cadet corps for instance. They use what is called gallery ammunition and the department have been selling this ammunition to these cadet corps for $3 a thousand. I understand that recently an order has been issued cancelling that arrangement and that the department will not now sell it to them.

Unfortunately we do not have it to sell. The quantity of that ammunition is dependent on the number of empty shells which are returned to the factory and we are not able to get anything like one quarter of the quantity we require.
The hon. minister will see that the department is charging these corps $3 a thousand.
It costs $5 a thousand.
I think a good many were under the impression that the department made a small profit even at that price.
No, this ammunition costs $5 a thousand and we were selling it for $3.

The rifle clubs are composed of men of all ages, men who are getting certain advantages from the Department of Militia and who will never be called upon to serve their country in the militia force. They are getting certain privileges that the boys who will be men in the course of a very few years are debarred from now.
We are able under this law to give them ammunition if we choose.
Will the hon. gentleman furnish the cadet corps that belong to the high schools with free ammunition?
I should think it would be a very desirable thing to do, but I would not like to state off-hand that it will be done.

We have some efficient cadet corps which are a credit to the districts to which they belong and I think the department should encourage them in this way. I think that in this appeal I will have the sympathy of the hon. member for La-belle who is strongly in favour of the boys becoming better shots.
The hon. minister promised to take two or three little suggestions.into his consideration to-day. I spoke of the drill and pay of the cadets corps.
I will consider that although I think that to pay young men in schools and colleges might not be desirable.

I refer to those who are permitted to go to camp. Paragraph (c) of section 73 of the Bill reads :
The minister may authorize senior cadet corps, or any portion thereof, to be attached to any portion of the active militia for the purposes of drill and training.
I presume that means training in the camps.
No it does not; it means that they may be attached to a regiment but not in camp.

I am advised that the cadet corps are looking forward with a great deal of pleasure to being permitted to attend the camp even for one day. The cadet corps even in my own district are looking forward, as other cadet corps are in No. 1 military district, to being able to attend the camp at London for at least one day.
Progress reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved that the House again go into Committee of Supply.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, it is eleven o'clock.

We have a notice to appear at a committee at 9.30 to-morrow morning. Does the right hon. gentleman expect that we can come here at eleven o'clock in the morning, remain here performing our duties until eleven o'clock at night and be here again at 9.30 to-morrow morning ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That seems reasonable.
Motion withdrawn.
On motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, House adjourned at 11 p.m.

Wednesday, July 13, 1904.
